title: The eco-scam app, Astra's opacity problem, and writing in your own voice
tldr: A viral "eco-friendly" AI app got tagged a scam for reviving a debunked water-scarcity myth.
GPT-6 Astra's new "opaque recurrence" training method has safety researchers alarmed about lost transparency.
ChatGPT Work can now learn and reproduce your writing voice across Gmail, Slack, and Drive.

tips.heading: Make ChatGPT Work write in your voice
steps: Open ChatGPT, toggle on Work, then go to Settings > Personalization > Writing Style.
Connect the apps with the best examples of your writing, such as Gmail, Google Drive, and Slack.
Let ChatGPT analyze the patterns in your writing, then return to Work and ask it to draft an email, message, or document as usual.
Review the output to confirm it sounds like you, and adjust the connected sources if it doesn't.

news.body: Viral "eco-friendly" AI app draws scam accusations. EcoGPT has been downloaded more than 100,000 times on the back of videos claiming AI data centers will make fresh drinking water disappear, a claim Superhuman AI says has been "repeatedly debunked." Critics are now calling the app a scam that uses greenwashing to exploit environmental guilt.
news.means: Expect this specific water-scarcity myth to keep resurfacing in client conversations about AI's environmental cost; worth having the debunk ready rather than letting it pass unchallenged.

news.body: GPT-6 Astra's efficiency trick worries AI safety researchers. Reporting ties Astra to a training method called "recurrent depth" (or "opaque recurrence"), which cycles a query through the same internal layers repeatedly instead of reasoning in visible steps. Redwood Research's chief scientist Ryan Greenblatt called it "the single worst development for AI security/safety to date," though OpenAI says Astra's chain of thought "remains largely readable" for now.
news.means: Chain-of-thought transparency is a selling point vendors use in AI-governance pitches; this is an early sign providers may trade it away for performance, worth flagging in any client AI-risk discussion.
